notes.made: David Foster and Jay Graydon wrote the music and Bill Champlin the words. Foster first ad-libbed the chorus during sessions for a Jaye P. Morgan album, Tommy Mottola says Hall & Oates turned it down, and Champlin had pencilled it in for his own solo record before Foster and Graydon told him it was going to EWF. Maurice White produced it and changed the title from After the Love Is Gone. I Am was cut between September 1978 and March 1979 at Hollywood Sound, Sunset Sound and Davlen, engineered by George Massenburg, with Maurice White singing lead, Philip Bailey on backing vocals, Larry Dunn on keys, Jerry Hey arranging the horns, Foster arranging the strings and Don Myrick on alto sax.
notes.context: Released in July 1979, the summer disco was being booed out of ballparks, from an album whose other big single, Boogie Wonderland, was the band's dance record. It got to 2 on both the Hot 100 (stuck behind the Knack's My Sharona) and the soul chart, and 4 in the UK. At the February 1980 Grammys it lost Record and Song of the Year to What a Fool Believes and won Best R&B Song and Best R&B Vocal Performance by a Duo or Group.

listen_for.note: Don Myrick's alto saxophone solo over the Foster and Graydon changes.
Maurice White's lead with Philip Bailey stacked in the backing vocals.
Foster's string arrangement and Jerry Hey's horn chart. Hey plays trumpet on the album too.

leads_to.title: After the Love Is Gone
leads_to.why: Foster and Graydon's own band cutting the song under its original title, with Bill Champlin singing and Jeff Porcaro on drums. Graydon calls it the original version.

notes.unverified: No studio is given per track, only for the album. Panel line (Foster, Graydon and Champlin wrote it) is correct.

culture.title: Number 2, twice
culture.line: Released in July 1979, it peaked at 2 on the Hot 100, behind the Knack's My Sharona, and at 2 on the R&B chart. It made 4 in the UK.

culture.title: Two Grammys, two losses
culture.line: On 27 February 1980 it lost Record and Song of the Year to What a Fool Believes and won Best R&B Song and Best R&B Vocal Performance by a Duo or Group.

culture.title: Airplay
culture.line: Foster and Graydon's own band Airplay cut it as After the Love Is Gone on their February 1980 album, with Bill Champlin singing and Jeff Porcaro drumming.
